lessons.sourceTitleEnglish: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Say what you have, need and want at the table and ask if there is a table or a wait.
lessons.sourceSpeakingEnglish: Ask the host if there is a table for your group, say you have a reservation, and ask if you have to wait.
lessons.title: Tables, Reservations, Needs, and Wants
lessons.objective: Ask whether a table is available, state a reservation, say what the group needs, and ask whether there will be a wait.
lessons.focus: 席はありますか asks whether seats are available; 予約があります states that you have a reservation. いすが必要です says a chair is needed, while 〜がほしいです expresses wanting an item. 待たなければなりませんか asks whether waiting is necessary. These functions replace the Spanish tener/hay/querer pattern.
lessons.scene: Sam arrives with a party of two and asks the host about their reservation and a chair.

lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Say where you are going, what you plan to do and ask what you can do at dinner.
lessons.sourceSpeakingEnglish: Tell the host you are going to wait at the bar and that you are going to celebrate something, then ask if you can make a toast.
lessons.title: Plans, Possibility, and a Toast
lessons.objective: Say where you will wait, describe a celebration plan, and ask whether a toast or a food change is possible.
lessons.focus: バーで待ちます states where you will wait; 〜する予定です marks a plan. 乾杯してもいいですか asks permission for a toast, while できますか asks whether the kitchen can make a dish a certain way. 食後のおしゃべり describes conversation after dinner without treating Spanish sobremesa as a Japanese loanword.
lessons.scene: At an anniversary dinner, Sam and Lea wait at the bar, ask about a garlic-free fish, and make a toast.

lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Say what you and others eat, drink and share using present-tense verbs.
lessons.sourceSpeakingEnglish: Tell a dining companion what you eat and drink, ask what they eat, and say what you are sharing.
lessons.title: What We Eat, Drink, and Share
lessons.objective: Use Japanese polite present forms to say what people eat and drink, ask about seafood and soup, and say what the group shares.
lessons.focus: 食べます and 飲みます are polite non-past verbs for eating and drinking. 分けます says the group shares; 食べますか forms a question with か. Japanese does not have separate Spanish -ar/-er/-ir verb classes, and context tells whether a non-past form describes a habit or a current choice. 魚介類 means seafood broadly, while 貝類 is specifically shellfish.
lessons.scene: At dinner, Sam and Lea discuss seafood, sparkling water, a shared salad, and a soup ingredient.

internalReviewNotes: Qualified Japanese review is required for polite register, counters, kanji readings, restaurant usage, and variant answers.
The source functions of have/exist/need/want, plan/can, and present-tense eat/drink/share are preserved through Japanese-specific grammar, not Spanish conjugation labels.
Dinner scenes are fictional; no meal, ingredient, or restaurant claim is presented as universal.
